readings.c1s1:
{{smaller block|<poem>Rumour will ''voice'' me the contempt of manhood,
Should I run on thus. {{right|''Ford'', Broken Heart, iii. 2.}}</poem>}}
'''5.''' In ''phonetics'', to utter with voice or tone or sonancy, as distinguished from breath.

'''II.†''' ''intrans.'' To speak; vote; give opinion.
{{smaller block|I remember, also, that this place [Acts xvi.] is pretended for the people’s power of ''voicing'' in councils.
{{right|''Jer. Taylor'', Episcopacy Asserted, § 41.}}}}

'''voiced''' (voist), ''a.'' [< ''voice'' + ''-ed''<sup>2</sup>.] Furnished with a voice: usually in composition: as, sweet-''voiced.''
{{smaller block|<poem>That ’s Erythæa,
Or some angel ''voic’d'' like her.</poem>
{{right|''Sir J. Denham'', The Sophy. (''Latham.'')}}}}

'''voiceful''' (vois′fu̇l), ''a.'' [< ''voice'' + ''-ful.''] Having a voice; vocal; sounding.
{{smaller block|<poem>The seniors then did bear
The ''voiceful'' heralds’ sceptres, sat within a sacred sphere,
On polish’d stones, and gave by turns their sentence.</poem>
{{right|''Chapman'', Iliad, xviii. 459.}}
<poem>The swelling of the ''voiceful'' sea.</poem>
{{right|''Coleridge'', Fancy in Nubibus.}}}}

'''voicefulness''' (vois′fu̇l-nes), ''n.'' The property or state of being voiceful; vocality.
{{smaller block|In the wilds of these isles one drinks in the spirit of the sea, and its deep ''voicefulness'' fills the air.
{{right|''Portfolio'', N. S., IX. 187.}}}}

'''voiceless''' (vois′les), ''a.'' [< ''voice'' + ''-less.''] '''1.''' Having no voice, utterance, or vote; mute; dumb.
{{smaller block|The proctors of the clergy were ''voiceless'' assistants.
{{right|''Coke.'' (''Latham.'')}}
<poem>Childless and crownless, in her ''voiceless'' woe.</poem>
{{right|''Byron'', Childe Harold, iv. 79.}}}}
'''2.''' In ''phonetics'', not voiced or sonant; surd.

'''voicelessness''' (vois′les-nes), ''n.'' The state of be-
readings.c1s2:
ing voiceless; silence.

¶
'''voice-part''' (vois′pärt), ''n.'' See ''part'', 5, and ''part-writing''.

'''voicer''' (voi′sėr), ''n.'' One who voices or regulates the tone of organ-pipes.

'''voice-thrill''' (vois′thril), ''n.'' Same as ''vocal fremitus'' (which see, under ''vocal'').

'''voicing''' (voi′sing), ''n.'' [Verbal n. of ''voice'', ''v.''] The act, process, or result of regulating the tone of organ-pipes, so that they shall sound with the proper power, pitch, and quality. {{smaller|Voicing is the most delicate and important branch of organ-building, since success in it depends on attention to the minutest details.}}

'''void''' (void), ''a.'' and ''n.'' [< ME. ''void'', ''voyd'', ''voide'', < OF. ''voide'', ''vuide'', m. and f., also ''void'', ''vuid'', ''vuit'', m., empty, waste, vast, wide, hollow, also deprived, destitute, devoid; as a noun, a void, waste; F. ''vide'', empty, devoid; according to the usual derivation, < L. ''viduus'', bereft of husband or wife, bereft, deprived; but this derivation is difficult phonetically and in view of the existing F. ''veuf'', m., ''veuve'', f., widowed, deprived (as a noun, a widower, widow), from the same L. ''viduus''. The F. ''vide'' for ''vuide'', however, has been influenced by association with the L. ''viduus''. Another derivation, < LL. as if *''vocitus'' for *''vacitus'', akin to ''vacare'', be empty, ''vacuus'', empty, ''vacivus'', ''vocivus'' (see ''vacuous'', vacant), rests on assumption. Cf. ''avoid'', ''devoid''.] '''I.''' ''a.'' '''1.''' Empty, or not containing matter; vacant; not occupied; unfilled: as, a ''void'' space or place.
{{smaller block|And he that shall a-complysshe that sete must also complysshe the ''voyde'' place at the table that Ioseph made.
{{right|''Merlin'' (E. E. T. S.), i. 61.}}}}

Should I run on thus. {{right|''Ford'', Broken Heart, iii. 2.}}</poem>}}
'''5.''' In ''phonetics'', to utter with voice or tone or sonancy, as distinguished from breath.

{{smaller block|In the wilds of these isles one drinks in the spirit of the sea, and its deep ''voicefulness'' fills the air.

{{smaller block|The proctors of the clergy were ''voiceless'' assistants.

{{smaller block|<poem>Childless and crownless, in her ''voiceless'' woe.</poem>
{{right|''Byron'', Childe Harold, iv. 79.}}}}

'''void''' (void), ''a.'' and ''n.''   [< ME. ''void'', ''voyd'', ''voide'', < OF. ''voide'', ''vuide'', m. and f., also ''void'', ''vuid'', ''vuit'', m., empty, waste, vast, wide, hollow, also deprived, destitute, devoid; as a noun, a void, waste; F. ''vide'', empty, devoid; according to the usual derivation, < L. ''viduus'', bereft of husband or wife, bereft, deprived; but this derivation is difficult phonetically and in view of the existing F. ''veuf'', m., ''veuve'', f., widowed, deprived (as a noun, a widower, widow), from the same L. ''viduus''. The F. ''vide'' for ''vuide'', however, has been influenced by association with the L. ''viduus''. Another derivation, < LL. as if *''vocitus'' for *''vacitus'', akin to ''vacare'', be empty, ''vacuus'', empty, ''vacivus'', ''vocivus'' (see ''vacuous'', vacant), rests on assumption. Cf. ''avoid'', ''devoid''.]   '''I.''' ''a.'' '''1.''' Empty, or not containing matter; vacant; not occupied; unfilled: as, a ''void'' space or place.
{{smaller block|And he that shall a-complysshe that sete must also complysshe the ''voyde'' place at the table that Ioseph made.
{{right|''Merlin'' (E. E. T. S.), i. 61.}}}}
{{smaller block|The earth was without form, and ''void'' [was waste and ''void'', R. V.], and darkness was upon the face of the deep.
{{right|Gen. i. 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>I’ll get me to a place more ''void'', and there
Speak to great Cæsar as he comes along.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', J. C., ii. 4. 37.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>In the ''void'' offices around
Rung not a hoof, nor bayed a hound.</poem>
{{right|''Scott'', Rokeby, ii. 17.}}}}
'''2.''' Having no holder or possessor; vacant; unoccupied; without incumbent.
{{smaller block|The Bishoprick of Winchester falling ''void'', the king sends presently to the Monks of the Cathedral Church to elect his Brother Athelmar.
{{right|''Baker'', Chronicles, p. 83.}}}}
{{smaller block|A plantation should be begun at Agawam (being the best place in the land for tillage and cattle), least an enemy, finding it ''void'', should possess and take it from us.
{{right|''Winthrop'', Hist. New England, I. 118.}}}}
'''3†.''' Not taken up with business; leisure.
{{smaller block|All the ''void'' time that is between the hours of work, sleep, and meat, that they be suffered to bestow every man as he liketh best himself.
{{right|''Sir T. More'', Utopia (tr. by Robinson), ii. 4.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>I chain him in my study, that, at ''void'' hours,
I may run over the story of his country. ''Massinger''.</poem>}}
'''4.''' Being without; devoid; destitute; lacking; without; free from: usually with ''of:'' as, ''void of'' learning; ''void of'' common sense.
{{smaller block|The moste parte of noble men and gentlemen within this Realme haue bene brought vp ignorantly and ''voide of'' good educac[i]ons.
{{right|''Booke of Precedence'' (E. E. T. S., extra ser.), i. 10.}}}}

{{smaller block|Ye must be ''void'' from that desperate solicitude.
{{right|''Traves'', in Bradford’s Letters (Parker Soc., 1853), II. 3.}}}}

{{smaller block|He that is ''void of'' wisdom despiseth his neighbour.
{{right|Prov. xi. 12.}}}}

'''5.''' Not producing any effect; ineffectual; useless; vain; superfluous.

{{smaller block|''Voide'' leves puld to be.
{{right|''Palladius'', Husbondrie (E. E. T. S.), p. 150.}}}}

{{smaller block|Wyth bones & ''voyd'' morsels fyll not thy trenchour, my friend, full.
{{right|''Babees Book'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 79.}}}}

{{smaller block|My word . . . shall not return to me ''void'', but it shall accomplish that which I please.
{{right|Isa. lv. 11.}}}}

{{smaller block|The game [rocks of Scilly] is reckoned in the same manner as at mississipi, and the cast is ''void'' if the ball does not enter any of the holes.
{{right|''Strutt'', Sports and Pastimes, p. 398.}}}}

'''6.''' Specifically, in ''law'', without legal efficacy; incapable of being enforced by law; having no legal or binding force; null; not effectual to bind parties, or to convey or support a right: as, a deed not duly signed and sealed is ''void;'' a promise without consideration is ''void''. {{smaller|In strictness the word is appropriate only of that which is so utterly without effect that a person may act as if it did not exist; but a thing may be void as to some persons and not as to others. ''Void'' is, however, often used in place of ''voidable''. ''Voidable'' is appropriate for that which a person has the right to make of no effect by application to court to have it adjudged ''void'', or in some cases by notice or declaration, as a conveyance in fraud of creditors which is effectual between the parties, but may be avoided by a creditor, or a contract of an infant, which may be effectual until he has disaffirmed it. That which is void is generally held incapable of confirmation; that which is simply voidable may be confirmed.}}

'''7†.''' Devoid of wealth; poor. {{smaller block|Yif thow haddyst entred in the path of this lyf a ''voyde'' wayferinge man, than woldest thow synge byforn the thef.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Boëthius, ii. prose 5.}}}}
{{smaller|'''To make void''', to render useless or of no effect.}}
{{smaller block|For if they which are of the law be heirs, faith is ''made void'', and the promise made of none effect. Rom. iv. 14.}}
{{smaller block|<poem>It was thy device
By this alliance to ''make void'' my suit.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', 3 Hen. VI., iii. 3. 142.}}}}
{{smaller|'''Void for uncertainty''', said of a legal instrument the language of which is so vague or ambiguous that it cannot take effect.—'''Void space''', in ''physics'', a vacuum. ='''Syn. 1, 2,''' and '''4.''' ''Devoid'', etc. See ''vacant''.—'''6.''' Invalid.}}

'''II.''' ''n.'' '''1.''' An empty or unoccupied space; a vacuum.
{{smaller block|The ''Void'' of Heav’n a gloomy Horror fills.
{{right|''Congreve'', Birth of the Muse.}}}}
{{smaller block|The illimitable ''Void''.
{{right|''Thomson'', Summer, l. 34.}}}}
{{smaller block|I do not like to see anything destroyed, any ''void'' produced in society.
{{right|''Burke'', Rev. in France.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>What peaceful hours I once enjoyed!
How sweet their memory still!
But they have left an aching ''void''
The world can never fill.</poem>
{{right|''Cowper'', Oh, for a closer walk with God!}}}}
'''2.''' An opening; a solution of continuity in an inclosure of any kind; a space unfilled or not built up, as contrasted with closed or occupied areas.
{{smaller block|The clerestory window [of Notre Dame, Paris], . . . although larger than such openings had been in Romanesque design, . . . nevertheless is simply an opening in a wall, the area of the solid still being greater than that of the ''void''.
{{right|''C. H. Moore'', Gothic Architecture, p. 86.}}}}
'''3†.''' The last course or remove; the dessert.

{{smaller block|There was a ''void'' of spice-plates and wine.
{{right|''Coronation of Anne Boleyn'' (Arber’s Eng. Garner, II. 50).}}}}

'''void''' (void), ''v.''   [< ME. ''voiden'', < OF. ''voider'', ''voidier'', ''vuidier'', ''vuider'', F. ''vider'' = Pr. ''voiar'', ''voyar'', ''vueiar'', ''voidar'' = Cat. ''vuydar'', make void; from the adj. Cf. ''avoid''.]   '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To make or leave vacant; quit; vacate; depart from; leave; hence, to clear; free; empty.
{{smaller block|They ''voidede'' the cite of Ravenne by certeyn day assingned.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Boëthius, i. prose 4.}}}}
{{smaller block|Now this feest is done, ''voyde'' ye the table.
{{right|''Babees Book'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 271.}}}}
{{smaller block|Good Frederick, see the rooms be ''voided'' straight.
{{right|''Marlowe'', Faustus, iii. 4.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>If they will fight with us, bid them come down,
Or ''void'' the field.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Hen. V., iv. 7. 62.}}}}
{{smaller block|The princes would be private. ''Void'' the presence.
{{right|''Marston'', The Fawne, iii.}}}}
'''2.''' To emit, throw, or send out; empty out; specifically, to evacuate from the intestine or bladder: as, to ''void'' excrementitious matter.
{{smaller block|The place of the Welles and of the Walles and of many other thinges ben zit apertly sene; but the richesse is ''voyded'' clene.
{{right|''Mandeville'', Travels, p. 279.}}}}
{{smaller block|Whan the water was all ''voided'', thei saugh the two stones that were vpon the two dragons.
{{right|''Merlin'' (E. E. T. S.), i. 38.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>You that did ''void'' your rheum upon my beard,
And foot me as you spurn a stranger cur
Over your threshold.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', M. of V., i. 3. 118.}}}}
'''3†.''' To lay aside; cease to use; divest one’s self of. {{smaller block|<poem>He was glad of the gome, & o goode chere
''Voidet'' his viser, auentid hym seluyn.</poem>
{{right|''Destruction of Troy'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 7092.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>His locks, as blacke as pitchy night,
Were bound about and ''voyded'' from before.</poem>
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., VI. vii. 43.}}}}
'''4.''' To invalidate; annul; nullify; render of no validity or effect.
{{smaller block|It was become a practice . . . to ''void'' the security that was at any time given for money so borrowed. {{right|''Clarendon.''}}}}
'''5†.''' To avoid; shun.
{{smaller block|<poem>I ''voyde'' companye, I fle gladnesse.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Anelida and Arcite, l. 295.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>This was the meane to ''voyde'' theyre stryves
And alle olde gruchchyng, and her hartis to glade.</poem>
{{right|''Political Poems'', etc. (ed. Furnivall), p. 21.}}}}
'''6†.''' To dismiss; send away.
{{smaller block|He leet ''voyden'' out of his Chambre alle maner of men, Lordes and othere: for he wolde speke with me in Conseille. {{right|''Mandeville'', Travels, p. 137.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>So when it liked hire to gon to reste,
And ''voyded'' weren they that ''voyden'' oughte.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Troilus, ii. 912.}}}}
'''II.''' ''intrans.'' '''1†.''' To go; depart.
{{smaller block|With grete indygnacyon charged hym shortely without delaye to ''voyde'' out of his londe.
{{right|''Joseph of Arimathie'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 32.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Hit vanist veraly & ''voyded'' of syȝt.</poem>
{{right|''Alliterative Poems'' (ed. Morris), ii. 1547.}}}}
{{smaller block|Let all that sweet is ''void!'' In me no mirth may dwell.
{{right|''F. Greville'' (Arber’s Eng. Garner, I. 296).}}}}
'''2.''' (''a''†) To have an evacuation.
{{smaller block|Here, for example, is “the memorable and prodigious history of a girl who for many years neither ate nor slept nor ''voided.''” {{right|''Pop. Sci. Mo.'', XXXVI. 544.}}}} (''b'') To be emitted or evacuated.   ''Wiseman'', Surgery. [Rare.]—'''3†.''' To become empty or vacant.
{{smaller block|Hit is wel oure entent whanne any sucche benefice ''voydeth'' of oure yifte yat ye make collacion to him y<sup>r</sup> of.
{{right|''Henry V.'' (Ellis’s Hist. Letters, I. 71).}}}}

'''voidable''' (voi′dạ-bl), ''a.''   [< ''void'' + ''-able.'']   '''1.''' Capable of being voided or evacuated.—'''2.''' In ''law'', such that some person has a right to have it annulled. See ''void'', ''v. t.'', 6.
{{smaller block|Such administration is not void, but ''voidable'' by sentence.
{{right|''Ayliffe'', Parergon.}}}}
'''Voidable contract.''' {{smaller|See ''contract.''}}

'''voidance''' (voi′dans), ''n.''   [< ME. ''voidaunce'', < OF. ''voidance'', < ''voider'', make void: see ''void'', ''v.'']   '''1.''' The act of voiding or emptying.
{{smaller block|''Voydaunce'' (or voydynge), vacacio, evacuacio.
{{right|''Prompt. Parv.'', p. 511.}}}}
'''2.''' The act of casting away or getting rid.
{{smaller block|What pains they require in the ''voidance'' of fond conceits.
{{right|''Barrow'', Sermons, III. xviii.}}}}
'''3.''' The act of ejecting from a benefice; ejection.—'''4.''' The state of being void; vacancy, as of a benefice.—'''5†.''' Evasion; subterfuge.
{{smaller block|And therefore I am resolved, when I come to my answer, not to trick my innocency (as I writ to the Lords) by cavillations or ''voidances'', but to speak them the language that my heart speaketh to me, in excusing, extenuating, or ingenuously confessing.
{{right|''Bacon'', Letters, p. 137. (''Latham.'')}}}}

'''voided''' (voi′ded), ''a.''   [< ''void'', ''n.'', + ''-ed''<sup>2</sup>.]   Having a void or opening; pierced through; specifically, in ''her.'', pierced through {{img float|file=century v08 p0585 c3f1.png|width=82px|align=right|cap={{smaller|Azure a Saltier Voided Argent.}}}} so as to show the field. {{smaller|When the word is used alone it generally denotes that only a narrow rim is left of the bearing described as voided. See ''voided per cross'', below. Also ''coursie'', ''viudé''.}}
{{smaller block|All [spangles] are ''voided:'' that is, hollow in the middle, with the circumference not flat but convex. . . . Our present spangles, in the flat shape, are quite modern.
{{right|''S. K. Handbook of Textile Fabrics'', p. 93.}}}}

{{smaller|'''Voided of the field.''' See ''castle'', 2.—'''Voided per cross,''' in ''her.'', having an opening of the shape of a plain cross cut through it, so as to show the field. See cut under ''cleché''.—'''Voided per pale,''' in ''her.'', having an opening extending palewise, so as to show the field.}}

'''voider''' (voi′dėr), ''n.''   [Early mod. E. ''voyder'', < ME. ''voider''; < OF. ''vuideur'', a voider, emptier, < ''vuidier'', etc., make void: see ''void'', ''v.'']   '''1.''' One who or that which voids or annuls; one who vacates or empties.—'''2.''' Formerly, a tray or basket for carrying away utensils, dishes, etc., no longer required; especially, a tray or basket in which broken meat was carried from the table.
{{smaller block|See ye haue ''Voyders'' ready for to auoyd the Morsels that they doe leaue on their Trenchours.
{{right|''Babees Book'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 67.}}}}
{{smaller block|The fool carries them away in a ''voider''.
{{right|''Middleton'', No Wit like a Woman’s, ii. 3.}}}}
{{smaller block|Enter . . . servingmen . . . with a ''Voyder'' and a wooden Knife to take away all.
{{right|''Heywood'', Woman Killed with Kindness.}}}}
'''3.''' A clothes-basket.   ''Halliwell.'' [Prov. Eng.]—'''4†.''' A means of avoiding; in the following<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
